transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-22
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 55m
Attendees: Jamie Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Alex Rivera (Zelos VP Eng), Maya Singh (Zelos SRE), Tom Brewer (Zelos Infra)
Links shared: deck - redwood-hosting-options-v3.pdf, bench spreadsheet - zelos-latency-bench-templates.xlsx, SOC2 packet link (redacted)

Summary:
Quick discovery to map Zelos traffic shapes and p95 goals, assess fit for hosted vs dedicated vs private, and agree pilot scope for token/sec streaming benchmarks and p95 profiling. Focus on cost tradeoffs for p95 spikes and multi-tenant isolation needs.

Topics:
- Current stack & where model inference sits in their path
- Traffic patterns, burst characteristics, p95 latency targets
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private constraints (data residency, network)
- Streaming token/sec and concurrent users, KV caching and prefix reuse
- Security requirements (SOC 2, SSO/SAML, KMS)
- Next steps: benchmarks, docs, pricing

Action items (captured above)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jamie Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining on a Thursday afternoon. Quick intros — I'm Jamie, AE on the inference team at Redwood, and Priya's our SE who will be running the bench configs if we go that route.
[00:15] Alex Rivera: Hi, Alex here. Quick context — Zelos is shipping an assistant inside our developer console, it's pretty latency sensitive especially for streaming completions. We're trying to decide whether to start on Redwood hosted and then move to Dedicated or go straight to Private because of data residency.
[00:30] Priya Nair: Nice to meet you Alex — Maya, Tom — curious about typical lengths and concurrency. That will shape whether continuous batching helps you or if we need single-request low-latency paths.
[00:46] Maya Singh: Hey, I'm Maya. A few things: our p95 goal for interactive flows is 300ms for end-to-end tokens (not including front-end rendering), and for some bulk summarization jobs p95 can be 2.5s, but those are async. We're most worried about the streaming chat where users expect near real-time.
[01:05] Tom Brewer: Also, we have bursts around product launches — think 3x baseline QPS for 10–20 minutes, and then a long tail. We'll need graceful fallback when capacity is constrained.
[01:20] Jamie Chen: That's helpful. So you're calling out a p95 300ms for interactive streaming. Is that model with context windows of say 2k tokens or more?
[01:30] Alex Rivera: We're usually around 1.5k context for chat plus a 256-token streaming response average. Worst-case prompts can be 4k. We want the system to hit p95 300ms for the steady-state streaming token steps, not the full generation time.
[01:48] Priya Nair: Okay — two separate metrics then: token-step latency (the per-token streaming latency) and overall completion latency. For token-step, we can often achieve low p95 on small contexts with hosted optimized kernels. For 4k worst-case, quantization and KV cache size matter more.
[02:06] Maya Singh: Can you explain the KV cache behavior? We currently do per-user long-lived sessions for chat. If the KV cache misses or is cold at the start of a surge, it spikes latency.
[02:20] Priya Nair: Sure — Redwood's runtime keeps KV cache per session in memory on the serving host. For Dedicated we can reserve pool capacity so cold-starts are rare; for Hosted we do adaptive prefix caching and we also have an optional fast warmup feature that pre-warms by keeping a small hotset in memory. But the effectiveness depends on your reuse patterns.
[02:40] Tom Brewer: That warmup sounds promising. How do you estimate cost for keeping a hotset?
[02:48] Jamie Chen: Cost impact is basically reserved GPU cycles and memory retention; in Dedicated it's predictable in the reserved capacity cost. In Hosted it's usage-based but we can show you a tradeoff curve — more hotset memory reduces p95 spikes but increases baseline unit cost. We'll send a spreadsheet.
[03:02] Alex Rivera: Sounds good. We're also strict on data controls — all inference logs must be locked down and cross-region replication is a no for some datasets. SOC2 and KMS are must-haves.
[03:15] Jamie Chen: We support SOC 2 and customer-managed KMS for Private and Dedicated. Hosted can be configured with encrypted transit+at-rest and we offer a bring-your-own-key option for some enterprise tiers. We'll attach the SOC2 packet and the KMS integration doc.
[03:30] Maya Singh: And SSO? We need SAML 2.0 for admin console access.
[03:35] Priya Nair: Yes, SAML SSO and RBAC are available for Console for Dedicated/Private. Hosted also supports SSO for org admins.
[03:45] Alex Rivera: On the performance side — what's your benchmarking methodology? We need token/sec numbers and p95 under concurrency and streaming token-step times.
[03:58] Priya Nair: We typically run three bench profiles: steady-state (long-run), burst profile (10–20 min surges with x3–x5 traffic), and worst-case long context. For streaming token-step we measure per-token latency across the first 1024 tokens and the distribution. We'll also run KV cache hit/miss scenarios.
[04:16] Tom Brewer: What about routing and graceful degradation — can you route to a cheaper model variant when overloaded?
[04:23] Jamie Chen: Yes — smart routing policies can fall back to compatible model variants (smaller quantized versions) or to a lower-tier region. There's also an auto-fallback that prioritizes keeping the stream alive even at lower fidelity.
[04:38] Alex Rivera: For Dedicated, what's the smallest reservation that still gives reasonable p95 numbers? We don't want to overcommit.
[04:46] Priya Nair: Practically, a small Dedicated pool (2–4 GPUs depending on model family) with autoscaling burst capacity usually covers mid-market traffic. For p95 300ms token-step on a modern 7B-ish model you could get away with 2 GPUs for moderate concurrency, but if you're doing many concurrent interactive sessions with 1.5k context, you'll likely need 4+ to keep p95 headroom. We'll propose a sizing matrix in the spreadsheet.
[05:07] Maya Singh: Can you quantify "moderate concurrency"?
[05:10] Priya Nair: Sure — for example, assuming 7B CPU/GPU behavior and standard optimized kernels, moderate concurrency might be 80–120 concurrent active sessions generating stream tokens at ~10 tokens/s each. That yields ~800–1,200 tokens/s total. But this is model-dependent.
[05:30] Alex Rivera: That aligns with our telemetry — baseline is about 200 sessions active, but only ~40–60 are actively generating at a given second, bursts hit 250 active. So we'd expect token/sec peaks around 2k maybe.
[05:45] Jamie Chen: Good to know. We'll model three scenarios for the spreadsheet: baseline, launch burst (3x), and catastrophic surge (5x). We'll also include cost per 1k tokens and expected p95 for each environment.
[06:00] Tom Brewer: One more question — network egress and VPC peering latency. If we use Private inside our VPC, what’s typical intra-VPC latency impact?
[06:09] Priya Nair: Private deploys avoid internet hops — typical intra-VPC tails are stable, but you'll still see processing time. We've seen <1ms added latency vs local infra in same cloud region but cross-region traffic will obviously add network latency. We'll need your network diagram to validate.
[06:26] Maya Singh: We'll share that. Also, do you support on-prem air-gapped? We have one regulated data set that may require it.
[06:33] Jamie Chen: Yes, we have an on-prem package for air-gapped usage; SE-led engagement required. It incurs a different licensing and support agreement.
[06:44] Alex Rivera: For the pilot, what's the minimum we can run to validate p95 token-step under streaming?
[06:50] Priya Nair: Minimum pilot is a dedicated week where we run your traces through three configurations: Redwood hosted (optimized kernels), Dedicated small pool, and Private single-zone. We instrument p95 token-step, end-to-end generation p95, KV cache warm/cold, and cost metrics. We can run synthetic traffic derived from your traces.
[07:08] Tom Brewer: And you'll need API keys and maybe some sample payloads.
[07:12] Jamie Chen: Yes — we'll send a secure upload link for traces and a short onboarding guide.
[07:20] Alex Rivera: We do have some concerns about transcription of PII in logs — if we run traces, can you scrub PII?
[07:27] Priya Nair: Absolutely; we can redact or hash PII in traces before they enter benchmark storage. For Private/on-prem we can keep everything customer-managed.
[07:36] Maya Singh: On fallback patterns: in the past we've had cascade failures with other vendors where fallback to cheaper model caused incoherent responses — how do you validate fallbacks?
[07:46] Jamie Chen: We recommend model-family compatible fallbacks and running a small eval set that checks coherence/quality delta. Redwood Optimize can run quality regressions on your eval prompts and raise alerts if fallback quality drops below threshold.
[07:59] Alex Rivera: Do you have SLOs for hosted p95 latency?
[08:05] Jamie Chen: Hosted has published performance profiles but SLAs on p95 are usually part of Enterprise contracts for Dedicated/Private. Hosted is best-effort; Dedicated can be SLA-backed with latency targets if you commit to reserved capacity.
[08:20] Tom Brewer: What's the typical measurement window for p95 in your reports? 5 min or 1 hour?
[08:26] Priya Nair: We usually provide both rolling 5m p95 and daily aggregated p95 so you can see spikes and steady-state. For SLOs you can choose the window that matters to you.
[08:36] Alex Rivera: Okay. Let's talk rough numbers: if we aim for token-step p95 50–80ms on steady-state for the 256-token responses, what does that imply?
[08:46] Priya Nair: 50–80ms token-step p95 is aggressive — typically achievable on smaller models and highly optimized kernels with local GPU memory for KV cache. For a 7B architecture with good kernels and low context, you might see 40–60ms; with 1.5k context it's more like 80–200ms depending on batch efficiency. We can try to approach that with quantized kernels and dedicated GPUs.
[09:10] Maya Singh: If we relax to 150ms p95, would that substantially reduce cost?
[09:15] Jamie Chen: Yes — allowing higher p95 gives more opportunities for batching and using smaller model variants as fallbacks, which substantially lowers per-token cost. We'll show cost curves.
[09:26] Tom Brewer: Any risk on streaming correctness if you quantize too aggressively?
[09:30] Priya Nair: There is a potential quality delta; Redwood Optimize includes quantization recommendations by workload. We'll run evals on your prompt set to pick an appropriate quant config.
[09:42] Alex Rivera: Great. For benchmarking, can we instrument token-level latencies? We need distributions, not just averages.
[09:48] Priya Nair: Yes, we capture per-token latencies and report p50/p90/p95/p99 and percent of long tail events. We can overlay your traces.
[09:56] Jamie Chen: Alright — to summarize next steps: we'll prepare the spreadsheet and three bench configs, send SOC2 and KMS docs, and set up a pilot week starting next Wednesday if that works.
[10:06] Alex Rivera: Next Wednesday (2026-07-29) looks workable. We'll get the traces and the network diagram to you by Monday.
[10:13] Maya Singh: We'll also pin down which datasets need air-gapped handling.
[10:18] Tom Brewer: Any gotchas we should be aware of?
[10:21] Priya Nair: The two common surprises: 1) underestimated context lengths causing KV cache memory pressure during surges, and 2) assuming per-user session reuse when sessions are actually ephemeral — both change sizing. We'll instrument and test for both.
[10:36] Alex Rivera: Noted. Also, please include a note about cold start mitigation strategies in the docs — we want the exact knobs.
[10:42] Jamie Chen: Will do — Priya will include cold-start mitigation and the hotset sizing guidance in her bench notes.
[10:48] Alex Rivera: Perfect. Anything else?
[10:50] Jamie Chen: No, that's it from our side. We'll send the materials and a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff. Thanks everyone.
[10:58] Maya Singh: Thanks all.
[11:00] (call ends)

Notes on transcript: occasional transcription artifacts observed (e.g., "KV chache" instead of KV cache, "SAML SSO" occasionally transcribed as "SAML SOS"), speaker labels assigned by Fireflies and sometimes overlap.
